1: Stats: Strength carries weight and feeds stamina. Constitution toughens the flesh. Dexterity turns blows aside. Intelligence widens the mind's pool. Wisdom buys time when time is the question. Perception sees what others miss.
Wisdom is patience, and patience is time. Every point of it above the common measure buys you another breath when the dungeon asks its questions.
Math sharpens steel. The arithmetic of the blow is also the blow itself.
Animal lore turns dead things into food. Read your prey before you read its remains.
Cooking is its own art. Heat changes everything. Even the worst flesh becomes useful if you understand the fire.
Science speaks in wands. Each device asks a question and answers, briefly, in light.
Grammar turns marks on a page into power. Speak the words rightly or the scroll burns to nothing.
Philosophy unmasks. Every item wears a name not its own until questioned.
Theology reaches up. A prayer at the right place changes more than the words alone.
Geography knows armor. Cloth that covered which land? Plate that held which siege? Knowledge tightens the strap.
History wears rings and pendants. What was worn at Pharsalus is not what was worn at Hastings. Each accessory has a homeland.
Economics opens what was meant to stay shut. The same trade that buys a pie can pick a lock.
Your body burns through its reserves with every step. When the hunger gnaws deep enough, it begins to take something more than comfort.
Press the question mark and let the dungeon explain itself. It is the beginning of wisdom for the newcomer.
A blade that slashes, a point that pierces, a weight that crushes, three answers to three different kinds of flesh. A warrior who carries only one is only a third of a warrior.
Some bodies resist a cold no warm hand can touch. Some burn brighter when frost should kill them. Read the foe before you swing.
Hunger is one clock; bleeding is another; the careful traveler counts both.
Treasures rest where they fall. Stand over what you wish to carry and coax it into your hands.
Stairs are landings. A floor that asked too much may yet be left behind for a moment of peace at the threshold.
Fire and cold are ancient enemies. A creature born of flame laughs at your torch but shivers before frost; what walks in ice melts before an ember.
The dungeon does not announce its traps. A careful eye and a slow step save more lives than a quick sword arm.
Some doors in the dungeon open only when you already know where you are going. Maps and memory are their own kind of key.
Your strength is the length of your patience. A burst of stamina is brief; an even pace lasts a floor.
The deeper you descend, the greater the peril, and the greater the prize. The dungeon rewards the bold who survive long enough to claim it.
Death does not erase what you have learned. The questions you missed yesterday become familiar by tomorrow.
You should know better than to pick up a duck in a dungeon.
Fountains: A fountain in the dark asks a question before it gives anything. Those who answer badly have found poison in the cup, or company.
Graves: The dead are buried with what they valued. Now and then they are buried with something that is still awake.
Thrones: An empty throne judges whoever sits in it. The well-read have risen from it stronger. The rest have risen quickly.
Rooms: The sounds on arriving at a new floor are an inventory. Coins being counted behind a wall mean a strongroom somewhere on the floor.
Merchants: A small grey trader works the deep roads with a pack twice his size. Stand beside him and ask to see what is in it.
2: Pets: A small ivory sphere holds a soul. Hurl it with care and a companion is born, but the species that emerges is not for you to choose.
Pets: A companion fights at your side, and the longer you fight together, the stronger the bond. There are milestones of growth that change a creature, not merely strengthen it.
Pets: A wounded pet recovers slowly on its own. A patient owner can speed the healing if they have the right tools in their pack.
Pets: A pet that has learned to trust you has habits. Some hold the line; some patrol; some follow at your heel. The choice is yours, somewhere in a menu.
Identification: A small fragment of a greater Stone allows the careful student to see through disguise. Without it, the work is much harder.
Identification: Patience reveals what haste cannot. Some items hide more than a name, they hide a history, a use, and a gift to those who identify them.
BUC: Items carry a moral weight, sometimes hidden. A blessed thing helps more than its plain form; a cursed thing helps less, and binds.
BUC: Altars in the deep are not silent. A thing placed upon one will sometimes confess what it truly is.
Magic: A wand will fire whether or not you understand its history; a scroll demands you read every word; a spellbook is a patient teacher willing to share its lesson many times.
Magic: Mana is mind. The deeper the well, the longer the song. Drink rarely from a shallow well.
Prayer: A doctrine well-recited reaches further than a stammered one. The careful prayer rewards the careful student.
Prayer: An altar amplifies a prayer in ways that bare ground does not. Stand where the holy stood.
Karma: Your choices in the dungeon are heard. Mercy and cruelty alike are remembered, and remembered choices change what doors will open at the deepest descent.
Traps: A careful eye sees what the floor is hiding. Perception above the common measure shortens the wait between glance and glimpse.
Traps: Some traps can be persuaded to forget their target, and remember a new one. The right kind of cleverness flips a mechanism.
Wands: A wand of one charge is a single shot. Save the question for a worthy answer.
Scrolls: A scroll is one reading and then ash. There are exceptions, but assume the common rule.
Spells: A book that has taught you once still remembers the lesson. You will be glad of that when the next floor is harder.
Cooking: A meal is more than full bellies. Some dishes carry their ingredient's nature into you, for a time, or for the rest of the run.
Cooking: Two ingredients eaten together are not the same as two ingredients cooked together. The fire is a third thing.
Cooking: The dish is not chance. One question, answered rightly, turns crude flesh into the full meal.
Harvesting: Not every body yields food. The dead made of stone, dust, or fire will not feed you. Read what you killed.
Locks: A skilled hand and a steady mind can persuade a lock. The question is one of trade, what you would give to know what is behind it.
Locks: A merchant in the dark is a merchant still. He will haggle, if pressed by a clever tongue.
Stat training: A meal is not the only way to grow. Some moments at altars and shrines change you, and what they change tends to stick.
Combat: Every correct answer stretches your chain; a wrong answer freezes it. The strike lands at whatever length you reached, the higher the chain, the heavier the blow.
Combat: Material matters. The right metal makes the right wound, silver for what walks at night, iron for what slips through the cracks.
Combat: An armed shield is worth more than its weight in metal. The right blow turned aside is a blow you do not bleed for.
Equipping: Some armor and shields ask a question before they consent to be worn. The right answer is a fitting.
Floors: The odd tens are mazes and the even tens are thrones. Count the stairs and be ready for both.
Pets II: A creature kept fed and well-attended evolves further than one merely kept alive. The bond is the measure.
Discovery: A monster glimpsed is not yet known. Look long enough, study what its corpse offers, and the dungeon's record grows.
Death: Bones remember. A creature that killed you once may rise to oppose you again, in a form you would not wish to meet twice.
Heroes: The Maze-walker walked a labyrinth long before yours. The dungeon recognizes her descendants.
Heroes: Names hold power. To enter as another is to be welcomed in their honor, but the dungeon will not be fooled by a half-remembered name.
I know I shouldn't pick up that duck... but what if...
Altars II: An altar tells the truth to the kind and lies to the cruel. To those who are neither it says nothing at all.
Merchants II: The trader's first price is only an opening offer. The better the customer understands trade, the further it falls, down to half.
Prayer III: Heaven hears one great plea in a whole descent. Those who make it kneeling at an altar are asked gentler questions.
Mystery altars II: Some altars want an object before they will listen, and the object is never far away. Look in the other rooms.
Mystery altars III: A key carried past its lock is not always wasted. The same lock has been seen on more than one floor.
Unicorn: Somewhere in the first twenty floors grows a carrot that should not be eaten. Somewhere in the next twenty lives the reason.
Crucible: An alchemist's crucible wants lead before it will part with gold, and it likes to hear a little philosophy while it works.
Cauldron: The cauldron of the Head of Annwn would not boil a coward's food. The one down here is less particular, but it does expect three dishes.
3: Pet evolution: A bond is not a number. Time matters, but so does food, so does play, so does battle won together. None alone is enough.

Pet specials: At the second growth and the third, a creature unlocks abilities that belong to its newer form. These are not used the way a sword is used, they are commanded, and they cost the right answers.
Pet recall: A pet returned to its sphere is not lost. The sphere remembers, and what was hatched may be hatched again, with the same name and the same memory.
Pet feeding: A companion that eats from your stores grows faster, but you go hungrier. The trade is yours to weigh.
Identification: One philosophy question decides everything. Answer right and the item stands revealed, name, curse, enchantment, stats, and lore in a single stroke.
Identification: To identify one wand or potion is to know its whole kind. Every future copy you find will already carry its true name; only each copy's curse and enchantment still hide.
Magic: Some spells reshape the air itself in lines and cones and bursts. Read the description before you cast, distance and shape are part of the cost.
Magic: A spell that turns a creature against its kin is rare. Two enemies fighting each other are two fewer fighting you.
Cooking: One question decides the dish. Answer rightly and the recipe gives everything it promises; answer wrongly and the ingredients are gone.
Cooking: Special kitchens are not in the recipe book, they are in the player's memory. Combinations that feel right often are.
Cooking: Permanent gains from cooking have a ceiling. Beyond it, your body politely refuses to grow further. The fortunate cook plans the curve.
Cooking II: A pet eats what its master eats. To feed a companion is also to feed its growth.
Specials: Some powers do not live in a wand or a spellbook, they live in the bearer. A hero who has earned theirs uses them through a small menu, when ready.
Specials II: Special abilities are gated not by mana or charge, but by something older, a sustained recall of the right kind. The deeper the chain, the larger the gift.
Specials III: An ability practiced once is rarely a daily thing. Expect a cooldown matched to the floor's rhythm, one mighty deed per chapter, roughly.
Traps II: A trap rewired against its maker still consumes itself when it fires. Use it for the right enemy.
Traps III: A perfect understanding of a trap reveals more than the mechanism, it reveals something true about the dungeon. A piece of insight, like a hint, falls into the bearer's hands.

Prayer specifics: A prayer is answered in order. Breath first, then wounds, then the mind, then what is carried, then a shield. How far down the list Heaven reads depends on how well the doctrine was recited.
Prayer specifics II: A heart well-balanced and a chain well-built together produce blessings that neither alone could. Goodness and skill multiply.
Karma II: The judgment at the deep places does not weigh single actions. It weighs the long shape of a life. Plan your story accordingly.
Heroes II: A hero remembered with a full name is invoked more strongly than a hero remembered by a fragment. Some legends require their patronymic and their place.
Heroes III: The Hammer-bearer who walked the deep places carries a peerless rope; the Wolf-killer of the North wields a sword found in a haunted mere. Their names invite their gifts.
Heroes IV: Some heroes are themselves an answer to the dungeon's questions. The Strategist who took Tyre is not the same as the Strategist who escaped Sicily.
Items: A ring is rarely just metal. There are nine sisters in particular whose names recur in the songs, and what was true in song is sometimes true here.
Items II: A torch made by a Titan is not a torch. Some gifts ask for their bearer's blood as payment.
Items III: An armor cut from a hide that nothing could pierce is itself unpierceable. Find the lion and you find the legend.
Materials: Cold iron does to the Fair Folk what no other iron will. The fey-touched feel the chill even on a summer night.
Materials II: Silver knows the difference between the living and the unholy. A wolf at full moon is a different creature beneath a silver edge.
Materials III: Some metals are too rare for the curriculum: orichalcum, adamant, mithril. When you find them, you will know.
Boss F20: A horned king rules a maze, and its walls are no trouble to him. A princess of Crete once handed a stranger something small that made the maze fair. It was not a sword.
Boss F40: A gaze freezes flesh. Look away, or come prepared to see without seeing.
Bosses generally: Every twentieth floor belongs to someone with a name, and each name comes with a story about how it ended. The stories are worth knowing before the door.
Quests: A spool of golden thread in the deep dark is more than decoration. It is a promise of an exit.
Quests II: A bull cast in bronze is no use in a pack. Minos owed his bull to the sea and kept it. Some debts can still be paid in water.
Quests III: An eye, milky white, lost by the three sisters who shared one, is not a souvenir. Returned, it opens roads.
Identification III: A creature studied at the corpse becomes known by its kind. Once known, future corpses of the same kind no longer need study.
Lore: A monster studied is a monster read. Its weaknesses are written in the dossier for the hunter who looks.
Pets V: A pet that loves you sees nothing as cursed; pets that love their master would still rather avoid the cursed gear lying on the floor.

Quirks: There are dozens of small habits the dungeon notices. A hundred consecutive math chains; a hundred meals never spoiled; a hundred floors descended with no stair-rest. Each habit, perfected, has a name and a small reward.
NPCs: The dungeon's people are not all the same. Some are merchants, some are storytellers, some are tempters. Read them before you answer.
NPCs II: A tempter is rarely obvious. A bargain that feels too rich at the moment of offering is usually exactly that.
Cooking III: A meal that confers a stat does so once for each level of that stat, and then no more. The body has a ceiling for what food alone can build.
Stamina: The hungry warrior fights weaker than the well-fed one. Tend the inner fire as well as the outer.
Status: A burning enemy continues to burn after the strike. A bleeding one bleeds out across the turns. The patient archer can let the wound do the work.
Status II: Frozen things shatter when struck. Not always, but more often than warm flesh.
Status III: A poison is not a single dose. It is a slow argument with the blood, and it persists long after the bite.
Recovery: Standing on a stair on the way up is its own small rest. The bones stop singing.
Recovery II: Sleep is dangerous in the dungeon, but a stair landing is no monster's road. There the body knits.
Some say the duckie carries a tutor in patience. Most who proved the rumor were never seen without it.
Pandora: The box that says 'Do not open' has a good lock on it. Hope was never found by anyone who picked it cleanly.
Mimir: Odin paid for his drink at the well before he tasted it, and nobody offered him the eye back.
Fisher King: Percival sat at the wounded king's table and was too polite to ask the question. He was not invited twice.
Sphinx: The Sphinx of the deep is more patient than her sister at Thebes. She asks several riddles, each harder than the last, and forgives most of the wrong answers.
Fleece: The Fleece hung in a grove at Colchis under a serpent that never slept. It is beasts the serpent wants to hear about.
Forge: A dwarf-smith's work is spoiled by one missed stroke of the bellows. The unfinished hammer-head wants someone who can keep count.
Solomon: A king's seal found loose in the dungeon opens no door. It earns a hearing before an empty judgment seat, and the questions there are about the past.
Unicorn II: A unicorn will not be walked up to. Stand where she can see you, keep still, and let her decide.
Unicorn III: She has never taken food from a hand. The ground near her is good enough.
Unicorn IV: A unicorn knows what kind of traveler is standing in front of her. The cruel do not get a second look.
Cow: There is no cow level. Anyone who says otherwise has been bothering livestock, repeatedly.
Quests XI: The bronze bull and the fountain that wants it are not on the same floor. Neither are the eye and its altar, nor the broken sword and the god who broke it.
Quests XII: A shield that shows a face clearly does nothing from inside a pack. Perseus carried his on his arm.
Quests XIII: Medusa cannot harm what cannot see her. A blindfold is a desperate answer, and it is still an answer.
Quests XIV: A shovel is a poor weapon until something heavy walks across what it dug.
Quests XV: An old man with one eye told Sigurd that a single pit was not enough. He is seldom wrong about killing.
4: Recall: Some special abilities are not commanded by combat keys but by a small menu the player keeps. The bearer chooses; the dungeon receives.
Naming: Some companions earn names. A name once given is remembered through descent, through return, through the sphere that holds the soul.

Identification: The question follows the item. Gear is asked at its own tier; a scroll or wand at the harder of its reading level and the depth it belongs to; and no unique is ever asked below the fourth tier.
Curses: Some bearers know cursed gear as kin. They feel no diminishment from a thing the world has marked as ill, they only see the gift beneath the warning.
Frailty: When a man is at his lowest, his hand grows steadier and his teeth bare. Some wills lift higher the closer the body comes to falling.

Demigods: A man dipped in the river by his mother is unlike other men. His skin throws off a portion of the world's harm, except in one place, which legend remembers and which the dungeon does not always grant.
Witchers: A mutant child grown to silver-bladed adulthood is built against the unnatural. He carries his protection in his blood as well as his coat.
Elder Blood: The last of a doomed dynasty steps between places when the world closes around her. Such a woman is hard to corner.
Boss F60: A dragon lies on a hoard at the third great depth, and his scales turn every edge. The man who killed him spent longer digging than fighting.
Boss F80: A wolf waits at the fourth great depth, and he grows angrier the longer the fight runs. The gods never beat him by strength. They used a ribbon once, and they are keeping a shoe for later.
Quests V: A worn parchment in red-brown ink, scented of old fires, is not for the unsteady. Some pages should not be read until you are ready to be the page that turns.
Quests VI: An ancient tablet with a slot in its center is unfinished. The slot is shaped for something luminous you may already carry, or may yet find.
Quests VII: The bones of a giant wolf will not stay still under the floor. Six things, patient and unlikely, are needed to bind him. A cat's footstep is one. A woman's beard is another.
Quests VIII: The silent god's shoe is made of what cobblers throw away, and it has been a long time in the making. It was never meant for walking in.
Quests IX: The Scales of an Archangel hang somewhere in the deep places. They weigh souls, but they have other uses. Their bearer is not abandoned.
Quests X: A blade of white fire waits where it can be needed most. It knows its bearer by the way they carry their accumulated kindnesses.
Heroes V: The Trickster of Ithaca walks with a hood and a longbow. His arrows know the way home; his words know the way past.
Heroes VI: The Cynic of Sinope wants nothing. He travels light, sometimes too light, and his Lantern shines on whatever he chooses to seek.
Heroes VII: The Sword Saint of Niten Ichi-Ryū wields two blades. He grew up in a country far from this one, but his style works here.
Heroes VIII: The Maid of Domrémy hears voices. They are sometimes loud. Her standard restores the rallying spirit.
Heroes IX: The Detective of Baker Street solves the dungeon as a problem in want of attention. Every trap a fingerprint; every monster a chemical trace.
Heroes X: The first programmer's daughter sees a monster as a procedure, and procedures can be paused.
Heroes XI: A polymath of Vinci sketches things into being for a little while. His helpers are mechanical and remarkably useful.
Heroes XII: The Iceni Queen does not break. The harder the dungeon hits her, the harder she hits back.
Heroes XIII: The Abbess of Bingen carries the greening power of life. Her presence is a kind of cure even before she speaks.
Heroes XIV: The Wizard of Menlo Park is a circuit. What touches him touches itself.
Pet types I: Four kinds emerge from the common sphere, one electric, one watery, one verdant, one fiery. Each has its own specialty at each stage.
Pet types II: A holy hound called the Wolf-Devourer answers only to those who have spoken to the dungeon's hidden program. He fights well above his weight.
Pet types III: An ethereal Unicorn is a healer and a sentinel. She does not fight, but the dungeon's enemies cannot bring themselves to strike her.
Specials IV: Some powers cost more than their cooldown, they cost a strip of your own flesh. The Firebearer's gift, in particular, is paid in liver.
Specials V: A king of Sparta in the long defense calls on a stand. While the stand holds, the king's defense is doubled and his enemies' blows return in kind.
Specials VI: The Strategist who took Persia calls fear into the visible enemies. Bosses laugh at fear.
Specials VII: The Trickster of Ithaca turns a foe to friend for a time. Not bosses; never bosses. They are loyal to themselves.
Specials VIII: The thrice-great Messenger steps through space. The deeper the chain, the further the step, eventually further than the eye can see.
Specials IX: The Stagirite catalogues. The deeper the chain, the more of your pack he knows by name.
Specials X: A philosopher who questioned a city to death can question its monsters into confusion. Numbers and durations grow with the chain.
Specials XI: A Samian's harmony heals; the deeper the chain, the deeper the cure.
Specials XII: A blade that catches Ares and Aphrodite catches lesser foes too. Some weapons stun more than they wound.
Specials XIII: The wolf-killing blade from a haunted mere strikes plain and true, and somewhat harder than its peers.
Specials XIV: A spear that never misses its first cast favors first strikes. Save the chain for the next blow.
Specials XV: A jackal-god's blade drinks the fallen. Each strike heals its wielder a portion of what it dealt.
Specials XVI: The Archangel's sword brings hellfire upon hellfire. Against the abyss it deals more than against ordinary monsters.
Specials XVII: The Maid's banner heals and crowns the next blow with half again its force.
Specials XVIII: The Maze-walker reveals the maze. The deeper the chain, the more of the floor opens to her sight, traps, walls, stairs, and the names of items unstudied.
Specials XIX: The Cynic walks past curses untouched by them. What was harmful to others is to him merely metal.
Specials XX: The Detective's deduction in a radius reveals not only traps but the names of things lying about, if she has the wit to read them at a glance.
Specials XXI: The Abbess's Viriditas heals and cleanses. The deeper the chain, the more debuffs flow out of you.
Specials XXII: The polymath's sketch summons a temporary helper. Its level rises with the chain, at the highest, the helper is dangerous in its own right.
NPCs III: A creature offering you a deal at a moment of weakness is rarely a friend. The deeper the dungeon, the bolder the bargain.
NPCs IV: The grey trader in the deep keeps no fixed prices, only opening offers. A customer who understands trade pays less than one who does not.
Bones: A run that ended badly leaves something behind. Future runs of the same kind may walk into it. The dead remember the living.
Mystery altars: Some altars are not for praying at. Each asks one thing and asks it once. Walking away costs nothing. A wrong answer costs the altar.
Specials final: The Wizard of Menlo Park's resonance is passive. What strikes him in melee strikes itself, briefly, in return. No menu needed.
A guildhall ledger entry, half-burned: 'Bearer of the duckie, two thousand and twenty-six turns; rewarded.' The next line is illegible.
Quests XVI: The dwarves once forged a ribbon from six things that do not exist. They are said to have left the list lying around, one item to a floor, through the sixties and seventies.
Quests XVII: The forge that can make the ribbon stands one floor above the last thing it needs. Dwarves do not build for the convenience of visitors.
Quests XVIII: Old cobblers swear that every scrap cut from a shoe goes somewhere. There are ten in this dungeon, and the first lies very near the top. Keep yours.
Quests XIX: The silent god keeps an altar one floor above the wolf. It wants leather, and it can count.
Quests XX: A sword broken by a god may be laid on his altar, and he will accept it politely. He once threw his own spear over a whole army to claim it. He respects the gesture.
Seals: Seven princes of Hell keep seven seals on odd-numbered floors from the eighty-third down. The stair below the judgment seat will not open for six.
Judgment: The scales on the ninety-ninth floor give nothing to a soul that weighs nothing either way. The lukewarm go down unarmed.
Judgment II: The altar of the scales answers to prayer and to nothing else, and it answers once.
Host: The scales call the Host only once, and the Host fights only locusts. Every locust the Destroyer raises after the call is met by an angel.
Reward scrolls: A sealed scroll taken from a named terror is worth more above ground than below. It may be read as often as the bearer likes, and it is meant for a father's eyes.
Oracle: The priestess over the smoking rift takes coin and answers in riddles about the habits the dungeon rewards. She is cheaper than learning them by accident.
5: The deepest descent: A small radiant stone awaits at the very bottom. Carry it back to the surface and the quest is done, that is the whole of the deal, and it is much harder than it sounds.

Endgame: The Destroyer commands the abyss. He is mentioned in a final book of an old religion, and his retinue is locusts shaped from his despair. Bring the strongest of your kindnesses; the dungeon has weighed them.
Endgame II: A blade of white fire is the answer to a creature of the abyss. The blade knows its bearer by their virtue, and refuses no worthy hand.
Endgame III: The Heavenly Host can be called once, to counter what the Destroyer raises. The instrument of the calling is heavier than it looks and bears the likeness of a balance.
Endgame IV: At the second-to-last threshold, you are judged. The judge is not new to you, he is the archangel whose name is on the blade. He sees what you have done.
Endgame V: The last chapter of the last book says what becomes of Death. A scroll in the deep carries the line. It matters a great deal where the reader stands, and who is standing there with him.
Endgame VI: A Stone of legend, set into a Tablet of legend, is a key. The maker of the Wrench understood that creation completes; the cook who said 'one thing not built but joined' was right.
Endgame VII: The ground shimmers on one of the early floors and quotes a verse at anyone who stands on it. Nothing happens there on the way down. Remember the floor anyway.
Endgame VIII: Seven seals hold the Pit shut, each kept by a prince of Hell on a floor of his own. The seals are not broken by lifting them. They break when their keepers fall.
Endgame IX: A creature that should be invincible has, in songs, a heel; in scriptures, a name; in the deep places, a particular weapon. The way to a great thing is rarely a single way.

Hidden: An old text adventure left a single word that took the player elsewhere. The word is in many places remembered, and the dungeon remembers it too. Try it when the floor is quiet and the moment is fitting.
Hidden II: The dungeon is a kind of program, and programs accept hidden inputs. Not every key on your keyboard does what you would expect. Try the ones that seem to do nothing.
Hidden III: When you have nothing left to lose and a word that should not work, type it. Reality has cracks.
Hidden IV: The first word is older than the dungeon. It comes from a maze game that ran on machines older than your parents. It is short and has been spoken so many times that it has a feel.
Hidden V: An old text adventure had a single hidden command that became the example for all later hidden commands. The dungeon's makers were not original here. Speak the word that became the example.

Hidden VI: The hidden door has tiers. The first opening is small. The second is larger. The fifth is something the bearer should not lightly invite. Wait until you can withstand what is on the other side.

Holy fire: A column of flame called down upon a particular tile of a particular floor is more than a spell. Some monsters, at that depth, are vulnerable to a brief reduction of their armor against the holy. The reduction does not last long.
Locust swarms: The Destroyer's swarms are summoned, not born. Each summoning has its source. Cut the source and the swarm slows.

Bones details: Your worst death is not always your last. A run that ends in a memorable way leaves a particular ghost, and that ghost is, in the strict sense, recoverable, but only if your next bearer can reach the same floor.

L99 judgment: The deeper the kindnesses, the higher the prize. The deeper the cruelties, the more the price. Both are weighed by the same archangel, and both are paid in the same currency: what waits at the bottom.
L99 judgment II: A saint cannot be hurried into being. The kindest path through the dungeon is also, in places, the slowest. The judgment knows the difference between effort and accident.

The philosopher's arc: reading enough scrolls, studying enough corpses, and identifying enough items advances your understanding across the whole run. Milestones at 25, 75, 125, 200, and 300 unlock lasting boons.

Career: The student of identification who works through enough items earns small permanencies, a point of intellect, a knack for the obvious, a sharper eye, a point of wisdom, and at last a mantle under which every aura is plain. The thresholds are deeper than they look.

Hidden builds I: Some heroes invoked by name carry a weapon that does not appear in the spawn tables. The boomstick of a deadite-slayer is one; the silver blade of a Witcher is another; the elven steel of a princess is a third.
Hidden builds III: The Pokémon master keeps a cap that grows his companions faster. Address him by the simplest hero's name he is known by; he will be glad of the address.
Iconic items I: A belt called Megingjörð gives strength as the wearer would expect, and slightly more.
Iconic items II: A ring called Draupnir multiplies what falls into the bag.
Iconic items III: A ring called Andvaranaut draws coin to its bearer; the more thoroughly its bearer learns its lore, the more.
Theology: The single God answers through saints, who are persons after death and intercessors before death. They are not gods. The dungeon is a Christian world and an honest one.

Theology II: One great plea may be made in a whole descent, and Heaven's answer to it is final either way. Made kneeling at an altar, the questions are gentle. Made anywhere else, there are five, and none of them are.
Theology III: The deepest judgment is by the archangel whose name is on the blade at the bottom. The blade and the scales are kin; the bearer of one is, often, the worthy bearer of the other.
Identify wrong at your peril: a failed identify stuns you for ten turns. The Shard punishes guess-spam.
Cooking caps: Permanent stats from cooking respect a per-stat ceiling that rises with the deepest floor reached. To balloon by feast is not the dungeon's intent.
Pet caps: A pet's growth has milestones at level twenty-five and again at level fifty-five. Both are hard to reach and meant to feel like real moments, not inevitabilities.
Trap rewires: A trap perfectly understood becomes a trap perfectly relocated. The bearer of the deepest chain on disarm also receives a piece of the dungeon's own secret.
Pets recall: A pet recalled to its sphere is bound to that sphere. The sphere goes into the bag. The next throw is not a random sphere.

Quizzes: The hidden subject is not animal, not science, not philosophy. It is the subject of unusual things, and it is the subject that quizzes the bearer when they reach for what should not be reached.
Quizzes II: Some special powers ask the unusual question. The bearer must answer well to receive the gift, but the gift is proportioned to the answer.
Karma final: The judgment at the deep places maps your karma to one of five outcomes. The two extremes are dramatic; the three in the middle are themselves graded. Plan the long shape of your run.

Hint: A hint is a riddle, not a recipe. The dungeon trusts you to do the rest of the work, through play, through pattern, and sometimes through a thoughtful conversation with someone who has done this before.
Hint II: When the lore well runs dry, sleep on what you have learned. A second pass at a floor often reveals what the first pass missed.
Hint III: Some hints contradict each other. They are not lies. They are statements about different bearers, different runs, different orders of priority. The dungeon is large enough for both.
Wear the duckie. Endure it. Speak softly to it. The dungeon's joke is not always at your expense - sometimes it just takes a very long time to land.
Death: Death does not wait at the bottom. He comes when the Stone starts upward, slow in the deep and quicker with every quarter of the climb, until near the surface he outruns anyone.
Death II: Four things are needed to end Death, and they lie in order of descent: a place, a tool, a verse and a tablet. The first is met long before it means anything.
Death III: A wrench that turns nothing still joins two things. One of them is not found until the last floor.
Death IV: The verse about the lake of fire names its subject. Reading it does nothing unless the subject is present, and standing in exactly the right place.
Death V: The place where the veil is thin lies near the top of the dungeon. So does Death's best speed. Whoever means to meet him there should arrive with the work already done.
Holy fire II: Six altars ring the Destroyer's hall. Each will burn for a prayer once.
Abaddon: The Destroyer is weighed before he is fought. What the scales found on the floor above decides how strong he is and how many he brings.
